title: Reading crochet pattern errata
subtitle: Finding and applying corrections to errors in published crochet patterns
excerpt: Crochet pattern errata are corrections to errors found in a published pattern after it has gone to print or live. Following a pattern with uncorrected errors leads to a piece that does not come out as described. Knowing how to find and apply errata before starting saves the frustration of discovering the error mid-project.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: A published list of corrections to errors in a pattern. Plural of erratum. Most pattern designers and publishers maintain a live errata document, updated as errors are found.
A mismatch between the number of stitches that should result from following the written instructions and the stitch count stated in parentheses at the end of the row or round.

content.text: Errata

are corrections to errors in a published crochet pattern. Even well-edited patterns contain occasional mistakes: a missing stitch count, a wrong round number, a skipped repeat notation. Finding the errata document before starting a pattern takes two minutes and prevents the confusion of following an instruction that does not produce the stated result.
Where to find errata
The designer's website: most designers have a pattern notes or errata page.
The listing where you bought the pattern: Ravelry and Etsy allow sellers to update the downloaded file and post notes.
Publisher websites: book publishers post errata on the book's product page when errors are found in print editions.
Ravelry project pages: other makers note errors they encountered in the comments or project details. Search the project pages for the pattern name.
How to apply errata
Download or print the errata alongside the pattern before starting.
Mark each affected instruction in the pattern (pen on paper; sticky note in a PDF) so you cannot miss it when you reach that point.
When you reach a corrected instruction, follow the erratum, not the original text.
Diagnosing an error in a pattern without errata
If you reach a point where following the instructions produces a
stitch count discrepancy
, the pattern may contain an error. Steps to diagnose:
Recount your stitches by going back through the row or round manually, not relying on your first count.
Re-read the pattern instruction. Look for a repeat notation you may have missed: a star, a bracket, or the phrase 'repeat from * to end'.
If the stitch count is still wrong after reading carefully, check the stated stitch count of the previous row. If that count was also wrong, the error may have started earlier.
Check the designer's errata, Ravelry project comments, or Ravelry forum for the specific pattern. Other makers usually report the error and the fix.
Common problems

items.symptom: The stitch count is off by exactly the number of stitches in one repeat
items.cause: A repeat bracket is missing from the written instructions, causing one full repeat to be overlooked.
items.fix: Work one additional repeat and recount. If the stitch count now matches, the error is a missing repeat notation in the original.

items.symptom: The shape described in the instructions does not match the schematic
items.cause: The written instructions contain an error in a shaping row that is not reflected in the schematic.
items.fix: Use the schematic as the authoritative source for dimensions. Derive the correct number of increase or decrease stitches from the schematic rather than the written text.

items.symptom: No errata can be found but the pattern clearly does not work
items.cause: The designer has not published errata, or the pattern is self-published and was not tested.
items.fix: Contact the designer directly with a specific description of the problem. Most designers are grateful to be told and will post a correction.

content.text: What to try next

Before starting any pattern from a book or magazine, take five minutes to search the publisher's website and Ravelry for the pattern name plus the word errata. If you find corrections, print them and work through the pattern with the corrections marked before you pick up the hook.
